newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Safrican police hold 110 after anti-foreigner march.
newsitem.headline: Safrican police hold 110 after anti-foreigner march.

text.p: South African police on Thursday arrested more than 100 marchers who were protesting against a wave of illegal immigrants.

Groups of young men, some carrying sticks and make-shift clubs, marched through Johannesburg city centre for the second successive day chanting slogans against street vendors from poorer neighbours such as Zimbabwe and Mozambique.
On Wednesday, several stalls were looted in a similar march and pavements usually bustling with informal street traders were noticeably more empty on Thursday.
Police said 110 marchers were arrested as the protest was unauthorised and foreigners had been intimidated.
"Marchers hassled some of the foreigners on the streets as they went though town in the morning, and by this afternoon we decided we had to act," said police spokesman Johan du Toit.
Many of the marchers are local street hawkers complaining about what they see as an invasion of their turf by illegal aliens, attracted by the jobs and relative wealth of South Africa's big cities.

South Africa is already straining to meet the rocketing aspirations of a black underclass freed from four decades of racist apartheid oppression, and foreigners are an easy target for accusations of job-stealing and crime.

Protestor Robert Marapyana said the march was intended to be peaceful, but he blamed the massive influx of foreigners for many of the ills assailing Johannesburg -- a city infamous for its high violent crime rate.
"They (foreigners) are taking business away from the South Africans and they also come here to sell drugs," he said.
Estimates show the country has more than two million illegal immigrants, mostly from Mozambique and Zimbabwe, representing about 15 percent of the national workforce.
A recent study on unemployment found that 79 percent of South Africans saw them as the main cause of joblessness.
The marchers' claims have struck a chord with many ordinary South Africans.

"The people of South Africa are supporting these marches... if the police want to arrest anyone let them arrest all those (foreign) drug dealers," said bystander Thabo Putu, a worker at the University of the Witwatersrand.

South Africa's African National Congress-led government faces political pressure to crack down on illegal immigrants, but is hampered by a porous border that is virtually impossible to seal. Wages from migrant workers in South Africa also play a key role in the regional economy.
Many neighbouring states aided the ANC in its long struggle against the former white state and would be dismayed at the removal of a key source of foreign-currency income.
